Live Analysis walkthrough
xrefcode.com / docs / cli / live-sched

$ xref live sched

by Alexander Panasenko · xrefcode.com
On this page
  1. Usage
  2. Arguments and options
  3. Examples
  4. Reading the output
  5. Limits

See where a running process waits rather than where it computes: the time each thread spends off CPU together with the user stack it blocked in, voluntary and preempted context switches, wakeups, and every system call with its count and latency (p50, p99, max). The off-CPU stacks are saved as an .xprof recording whose weights are nanoseconds, so profile report and profile diff read it like a CPU profile.

Usage

xref live sched [OPTIONS] --pid <PID>

Arguments and options

Options

--pid <PID>
Target process ID.
--duration <DURATION>
How long to observe, e.g. 12s or 500ms; also ends at process exit or Ctrl-C.
default 10s
--stack-bytes <STACK_BYTES>
User stack bytes copied at each switch-out, to unwind the stack the thread blocked in.
default 8192
--no-syscalls
Leave out system calls (they need the raw_syscalls tracepoints, readable by root).
--out <OUT>
Keep the off-CPU recording at this new path (.xprof, weights are nanoseconds off CPU), for xref profile report and xref profile diff.
--top <TOP>
Rows in each table of the report.
default 20
--json
Print the capture and the report as JSON.

Examples

Command
# Does an idle daemon ever wake up? Twelve seconds of its scheduling and system calls:
sudo xref -b daemon live sched --pid 1234 --duration 12s
# Where a request's latency goes, kept for a before/after comparison:
sudo xref -b daemon live sched --pid 1234 --duration 5s --out before.xprof
sudo xref -b daemon profile diff before.xprof after.xprof

A process that waits in poll with a 10 ms timeout and writes one byte each time gives:

live sched: 2000 ms, 1 threads (0 unattached), 0 lost and 0 undecoded records, stop duration
context switches: 197 (98.5/s): 195 voluntary, 2 preempted; wakeups: 194 (97.0/s)
system calls: 390 (195.0/s)
off-CPU: 1.97 s summed over threads
note: 1 waits began before their thread was attached and count from the attachment
system calls by total time:
  call                   count        /s  returned       total       mean        p50        p99        max
  poll                     195      97.5       194      1.96 s    10.1 ms    10.5 ms    11.0 ms    12.8 ms
  write                    195      97.5       195    299.9 us     1.5 us     1.4 us     3.2 us     5.6 us
off-CPU stacks by time (root -> leaf):
     1.97 s 100.00%  target:_start -> … -> target:main -> target:wait_tick -> libc.so.6:poll

Reading the output

  • Context switches are voluntary (the thread blocked: a system call that waits, a futex, a page fault on I/O, or it yielded) or preempted (the scheduler took the CPU from a runnable thread). A wakeup is a thread getting a CPU again after leaving it voluntarily, so an idle process that never wakes shows 0 of both.
  • System calls: count is the calls entered while observed, returned those that also returned. Latencies are of the returned calls, from entry to exit, waiting included, so poll with a timeout shows the timeout. Quantiles are kept in buckets within 1/16 of a doubling of each other.
  • A wait already in progress when a thread is attached counts from the attachment (the note: line says how many). A lost record breaks its thread's stream: no wait or call is paired across it.
  • Off-CPU stacks add up the time each thread spent off CPU after leaving it in that stack; the frames below the program's last one are named by library file and function (libc.so.6:poll): the call the thread waited in.
  • Threads that start during the capture are attached when xref sees them (every 25 ms), so their first records can be missed.

Limits

  • Needs root or CAP_PERFMON with tracefs access: the switch events count in the kernel, and system calls come from the raw_syscalls tracepoints (--no-syscalls leaves them out).
  • Who woke a thread is not reported; that needs system-wide scheduler tracepoints.
  • Every system call of every thread is recorded, so a process making millions of calls a second slows down while it is observed.
